item.title: Mathematician Who Waited 50 Years for Proper Credit for Her Work Has Died
item.description: At the Los Alamos National Laboratory, Mary Tsingou Menzel’s computer programming helped set the stage for chaos theory and other fields.
item.dc:creator: Ama Sarpomaa

item.title: Will We Ever Understand Dementia?
item.description: Since the days of Dr. Alzheimer himself, there has been a dream that severe senility might have an explanation — and a cure. The search for both has never been more urgent.
item.dc:creator: Robert Kolker
item.media:credit: Oliver Farshi for The New York Times

item.title: Big Controversy Upends a Contest About Microscopic Videos
item.description: Nikon announced that it had disqualified the winner of its Small World in Motion competition over how A.I. was used in his submission.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu
item.media:description: Nikon’s Small World in Motion competition is an annual video contest that awards the best footage captured through the lens of a microscope.

item.title: Cancer Vaccines Are the N.I.H.’s Next ‘Big Bet’
item.description: New details have emerged about an initiative that starts in December to fast-track the vaccines, similar to the successful push for the Covid-19 vaccine.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: Cancer vaccine research at the biotech company Moderna in Cambridge, Mass., which reported in August promising results that a melanoma vaccine increased the time before cancers recurred and increased the time before the cancers spread.

item.title: ‘Breathtaking,’ ‘Devastating’: Mathematics Reels After New OpenAI Release
item.description: Hundreds of new A.I.-generated findings moved the frontiers of higher math in a single day — dispelling any doubt that the field is forever changed.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:credit: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times
item.media:description: Experts say the cataclysmic upheaval to the field will affect students the most, especially graduate students on the cusp of becoming a part of this intellectual community.

item.title: Before Computer Science Became a Boys’ Club, Margaret Hamilton Wrote the Code
item.description: The woman who helped put astronauts on the moon was a software engineer when the field was not prestigious or lucrative.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson and Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, via Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: U.N. Warns Against Technology Used to Read Citizens’ Minds
item.description: A report by the secretary general warned that new technologies could be used to access and criminalize people’s innermost thoughts.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Moens
item.category: Human Rights and Human Rights Violations
item.media:credit: Francesca Jones for The New York Times
item.media:description: While neurotechnologies have become powerful clinical tools for patients with brain injuries, the United Nations on Thursday warned that future technologies could be abused by governments.

item.title: For Two Sisters, a “Biological Age Test” Measured More Than Their DNA
item.description: They thought it might explain why their health had diverged. Instead, it stirred up feelings that weren’t so easily quantified.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn and Annie Flanagan
item.media:credit: Vivian Dehning; photographs by Annie Flanagan for The New York Times

item.title: Was the Human Gut Healthier in Ancient Times?
item.description: The microbiome isn’t what it used to be in many parts of the world. The shift may be affecting the well-being of people in industrialized countries.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: The Underappreciated Benefits of Leaving Fallen Leaves Alone
item.description: To homeowners, fallen leaves look like work. To nature, they’re an investment, with tremendous value on the secondary market as invertebrate real estate.
item.dc:creator: Alan Burdick

item.title: What Are the Remaining Millennium Prize Problems?
item.description: OpenAI’s trove of new math results doesn’t fully solve any of these highly prestigious open questions, but it seems to make progress on some.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: A page from an 1859 manuscript in which Berhard Reimann formulated his famous hypothesis, one of the remaining Millennium Prize problems.

item.title: 21 Birds Are Found at Miami Airport Stuffed in Underwear and Hidden in a Belt
item.description: Two men, who arrived separately from Cuba days apart, each carried clutches of live birds concealed in their clothes, the authorities said.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Chao
item.media:description: A man who was detained at Miami International Airport on Sunday appeared nervous and had an “unexplained bulge” around his pelvis, according to a criminal complaint.

item.title: The National Hurricane Center’s Boss Keeps an Eye on the Storms
item.description: The director, Michael Brennan, oversees 45 federal workers, including hurricane specialists and meteorologists.
item.dc:creator: Johnny Diaz
item.media:description: Michael Brennan has been director of the National Hurricane Center since 2023.

item.title: As Flood Risk Increases in Himalayas, Nepal Builds More in Vulnerable Areas
item.description: The total footprint of buildings along flood-prone riverbanks in the Himalayas grew by half in recent years, a study found.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
item.media:credit: Jason Gulley for The New York Times
item.media:description: Flood hazards in Nepal include monsoon downpours, earthquakes and avalanches that send boulders tumbling into lakes formed by melting glaciers.

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, Whose Software Guided the Apollo Missions, Has Died
item.description: Margaret Hamilton, the first female programmer hired to work on the space project at M.I.T., was 90.
item.dc:creator: Trip Gabriel
item.media:description: Margaret Hamilton with printed computer code in 1969.

item.title: RFK Jr. Plans Vaccine Injury Initiative, Drawing Wary Eye From Experts
item.description: Vaccine safety experts say more research into the side effects would be welcome yet question whether the health secretary’s effort will be grounded in science.
item.dc:creator: Sheryl Gay Stolberg
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, testifying during a Senate health committee hearing earlier this year.

item.title: A Lab Worker’s Death Is Raising Plague Fears in Russia. What Do Experts Want to Know?
item.description: Missing details about the death of a lab worker, including the cause, are worrying scientists.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:description: Russian health officials have not linked the death of a lab worker to infection with Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.

item.title: A Public Health-Minded Senator Asks: What Comes After Trump and Kennedy?
item.description: Senator Patty Murray, a former chair of the Senate health committee, is forming a group of experts to examine how to insulate the C.D.C. from political interference.
item.dc:creator: Sheryl Gay Stolberg
item.category: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times
item.media:description: Senator Patty Murray, Democrat of Washington, at the Capitol last month.

item.title: Jonathan the Giant Tortoise Is 194 Years Old. He Just Had His Genome Sequenced.
item.description: Scientists have sequenced his genome for the first time, hoping the world’s oldest land animal can offer clues into the genetics of longevity.
item.dc:creator: Monique Brouillette

item.title: Trump Administration Delays Threaten Funding for HIV Research
item.description: The networks also develop treatments and preventions for other infectious diseases and were instrumental in testing the Covid vaccine.

item.media:description: Drawing blood at an H.I.V. clinic in South Africa last year. The research networks’ large footprint has enabled them to develop tools to prevent and treat H.I.V., including in marginalized or rare populations.

item.title: In Vienna and Beijing, the First Nuclear Clocks Begin to Tick
item.description: By measuring the squishing and unsquishing of thorium-229 nuclei, two teams created a new type of clock that could someday beat the precision of atomic clocks.
item.dc:creator: Dan Garisto

item.title: Russia Says It Found No ‘Emergency’ in Plague Lab
item.description: New information around the death of a lab worker, including a statement that she had been vaccinated against the plague, came as U.S. officials demanded more data.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sonne
item.media:description: The entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday. An employee of the institute died of a mysterious pneumonia.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry Is Awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai
item.description: The Nobel Committee recognized Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for solving a century-old mystery about molecules with mirror images. Their work is crucial for pharmaceuticals and carries clues to the origins of life.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency, via Reuters
item.media:description: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry during a news conference at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, on Wednesday.

item.title: The Start-Up That Wants to Build ‘Microrobots’ With A.I.
item.description: Atomic Machines is training artificial intelligence on materials and designs — and then using it to build tiny physical devices.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Christie Hemm Klok for The New York Times

item.title: OpenAI Releases Findings on 377 Math Problems, Further Roiling Field
item.description: After a previous solution angered mathematicians, the company characterized the new release as being more responsive to concerns about A.I. disrupting research.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang and Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: For 10 of the findings, OpenAI provided summaries of how the A.I. model came up with its solution. The average result took about three hours of computing, the company said.

item.title: Supreme Court Hears Boulder Climate Case
item.description: Monday’s arguments were highly technical. A decision about whether the case could move forward isn’t expected until June or July.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles
item.media:description: Demonstrators outside the Supreme Court on Monday.

item.title: Energy Firms Try to Squeeze More Power Out of Old Nuclear Plants
item.description: It takes a long time to build new nuclear plants. So, some U.S. companies are looking to get more electricity out of reactors that already exist.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer and Rebecca F. Elliott
item.media:description: Constellation Energy, the nation’s largest nuclear power plant operator, said it would spend more than $4.3 billion to refurbish 11 reactors at six plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Physics Is Awarded to Francis Halzen for Work on Neutrinos
item.description: The Nobel Committee honored Francis Halzen for his “vision and scientific leadership” of a telescope within the ice at the South Pole.
item.dc:creator: Aurelien Breeden and Katrina Miller
item.media:credit: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency, via Reuters
item.media:description: The Nobel Committee praised Francis Halzen’s “vision and scientific leadership” at the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a research project at the South Pole.

item.title: In Race With U.S., China Struggles to Recruit Foreign A.I. Researchers
item.description: China’s booming artificial intelligence sector has given local researchers good reason to remain in the country, but it has yet to lure overseas scientists despite a government push.
item.dc:creator: Zeyi Yang
item.media:description: Chinese A.I. companies like Deepseek and Moonshot have made a name for themselves internationally. But China still struggles to recruit foreign researchers.

item.title: Melting Swiss Glaciers Release Archaeological Treasures
item.description: Archaeologists are scouring mountain passes as artifacts from a bygone world all but tumble out of Switzerland’s shrinking ice.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong, Giacomo d’Orlando and Mira Rojanasakul
item.media:description: Fragments of wood found recently around a fast-melting ice patch in the Swiss Alps.

item.title: Why Cities and States Are Fighting Climate Change in Courtrooms
item.description: Faced with a president who has called global warming a hoax, officials have filed dozens of suits against oil companies to try to cover the costs of extreme weather.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick and Claire Brown
item.media:description: The case now before the Supreme Court could affect dozens of others. Protesters gathered on Monday as the court heard arguments.

item.title: Texas Pediatricians Face Paxton Investigations for Vaccinating Children
item.description: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate, has alleged a sprawling profit-driven conspiracy. Pediatricians say the accusations are an attempt at intimidation.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:credit: Kaylee Greenlee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Rachel examining a patient in Texas last month.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Is Awarded for Discoveries in Neuroscience
item.description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were recognized for their work on light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a technique that uses pulses of light to activate neurons in the brain.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson and Leo Sands
item.media:description: Thomas Perlmann, the secretary general of the Nobel Committee, speaking at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm on Monday.

item.title: What Are the Biggest Questions in Science Today? 100 Scientists Weigh In.

item.title: Are Babies Conscious?
item.description: By pinpointing when it begins in young humans, scientists hope to better understand what consciousness is, and how it arises, in all of us.

item.title: Scientists Warn of Another Unseen Risk From Fire: Ozone

item.media:description: Manhattan’s skyline obscured by Canadian wildfire smoke on June 7, 2023.

item.title: A Supreme Court Battle Over Climate Change Begins
item.description: The justices are about to hear a lawsuit that could determine whether the oil industry faces billions of dollars in liability for damages caused by global warming.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick
item.media:credit: Mark Makela for The New York Times
item.media:description: Boulder has sued Exxon and Suncor saying they should help pay for the damage caused by global warming in the state. A Suncor refinery in Colorado last month.
